The car came around the corner too fast, the way they always do, like speed itself is part of the message. Someone leaned out the window—I didn't even get a good look at his face—and screamed the word, that word, before something came flying through the air and hit the pavement a few feet from where I stood. By the time I registered what it was, they were already gone, taillights disappearing down the street, the sound of laughter trailing behind them like exhaust.

It was a hot dog. An actual hot dog, bunless, glistening slightly under the streetlight, lying there on the sidewalk like some kind of absurd offering.

"Okay, but is that even gaybashing?" Rusty asked, staring down at it with the kind of squint he usually reserved for crossword puzzles. "Or is that just, like, assault with a side of name-calling?"

I didn't have an answer. It felt like it should mean something—should sit heavier in the chest than it did—but mostly I just felt confused, and a little bit like laughing, and a little bit like crying, and mostly like none of it made any sense at all.

Josey, of course, had no such ambivalence. "A hot dog," she said, shaking her head with theatrical disgust. "They couldn't even commit. Didn't even stop the car. What, were they scared we'd chase them down? Four queers and a wiener, that's a fair fight, guys, come on." She nudged the hot dog with the toe of her boot like she was inspecting evidence at a crime scene. "This is genuinely the least effort I have ever seen anyone put into an act of hatred. I'm almost offended on principle. Put some muscle into your bigotry."

There's a particular kind of alchemy that happens after something like this—not quite fear, not quite defiance, just a scrambling toward the ordinary, like ordinary things might insulate you from whatever just happened. So we went back inside and somebody put on music and somebody else remembered they had a silk scarf that needed hand-washing, and within twenty minutes we were gathered around the sink discussing the merits of Woolite versus regular detergent, whether it really made a difference, whether anyone actually knew what "delicate cycle" meant. From there the conversation slid, as it does, into other adult anxieties—whether Josey's renter's insurance covered theft, whether interest rates were ever going to come back down, whether any of us would ever own anything larger than a houseplant. It was as if we'd collectively decided that the best response to being screamed at from a moving vehicle was to become, as quickly and thoroughly as possible, extremely boring.

Later, needing air, or maybe just needing to feel like the night could still hold something other than what it had already given us, we wandered into the sex shop next door. The owner looked up from behind the counter and smiled at us like we were old friends, like our showing up was the best part of her evening, and something in my chest unclenched that I hadn't realized was clenched at all. The dildos on the wall behind her were arranged by color in this cheerful, absurd gradient—cotton candy pink into orange into a blue so bright it looked edible—and there was something almost tender about the excess of it, the joy built into all that unnecessary color, a whole rainbow of silicone nonsense standing in direct, stupid, glorious contrast to the flat gray hostility of a car speeding off into the dark.

# The Great Hot Dog Incident

It was a Tuesday night in the Castro, which meant nothing was happening and everything was happening, the particular quality of a neighborhood that exists in a state of permanent low-grade celebration. Marcus and I had just left his apartment, arguing about whether Woolite actually worked better than regular detergent for his good sweaters, a conversation of such staggering unimportance that I want you to understand exactly the mental space we occupied when the truck rolled by.

It was a pickup, jacked up on those ridiculous tires that suggest the owner is compensating for something, and it slowed down as it passed us on Market Street. Two guys leaned out the window. One of them yelled something about faggots—unoriginal, the kind of slur you could set your watch to—and the other one, in what I can only assume he thought was the coup de grace of this whole operation, threw a hot dog at us.

A hot dog. Not even in a bun, as far as I could tell. Just the meat itself, sailing through the San Francisco night like some kind of pathetic, processed missile.

It didn't even hit us. It landed on the sidewalk about four feet away, bounced once, and rolled into the gutter with the saddest little wobble you've ever seen.

There was a full three seconds of silence.

Then Marcus said, "Did they just throw a Ballpark Frank at us?"

"I think it might have been Oscar Mayer," I said. "I couldn't see the label."

"This feels like it should be classified as littering before it's classified as a hate crime."

We were laughing so hard we had to lean against the building, this wheezing, gasping laughter that had nothing to do with finding it funny in the traditional sense and everything to do with the sheer, gorgeous absurdity of it. Two grown men had driven around the city, worked themselves up into whatever rage they needed to commit violence against strangers, armed themselves with a hot dog, and executed their plan with the precision of a blindfolded toddler swinging at a piñata.

"I need to call my insurance company," I said, still catching my breath, "and ask if 'attempted frankfurter assault' is covered under my renter's policy."

"Do you think they high-fived each other afterward? Like, 'nailed it, bro'?"

"They definitely didn't nail it. That's the whole point. It's currently rolling toward a storm drain."

We picked ourselves up, still snorting with laughter, and continued down the street toward Blow Buddies—no wait, toward the sex shop on 18th, the one with the window display that changed monthly like some kind of deviant Bloomingdale's. That night it was rainbow-colored, dildos arranged by size and hue in a gradient that would have made a paint store jealous, purples melting into blues melting into greens, all of it lit from below like modern art, because in a sense, it was.

Inside, the music was thumping, something with a beat that made the floor hum, and there were maybe a dozen people browsing with the kind of unhurried confidence of people who have never once considered that they should feel ashamed of what they're looking at. Someone was debating the merits of silicone versus glass with the seriousness of a wine connoisseur. Someone else was trying on a harness over their jeans just to see how it looked, turning to check their reflection in the mirror.

"You will not believe what just happened to us," Marcus announced to the room, general, unaimed, the way you'd announce breaking news.

"Gaybashing," I clarified. "With a hot dog."

The clerk, a guy with a septum ring and an encyclopedic knowledge of every product in the store, looked up. "Did it hit you?"

"No."

"Then it doesn't count. That's just, like, a hate crime attempt. You have to actually make contact."

"I feel like there should be a merit badge for surviving an attack this poorly executed," Marcus said, already moving toward the wall of dildos, running his finger along the display like he was shopping for produce. "Courage in the Face of Condiments."

"Bravery Under Processed Meat Fire."

The clerk was laughing now too, and somebody else had wandered over, wanting to hear the story again, and I found myself repeating it—the truck, the slur, the impossibly slow-motion arc of the hot dog, its undignified landing—and each time I told it, it got funnier, and smaller, and less like something that had happened to us and more like something we owned, a story that belonged to us now instead of to them.

That's the thing nobody tells you about being on the receiving end of hatred when the hatred is executed with such staggering incompetence: it deflates on contact. Those two men in that truck wanted us to feel afraid, wanted to remind us that we were vulnerable, that our existence in that neighborhood was provisional, contested, unsafe. And instead we were standing in a rainbow-lit sex shop, surrounded by silicone in every color of the spectrum, laughing so hard our stomachs hurt, already turning their violence into material for our friends.

I bought Woolite anyway, on the way home. Marcus's sweaters needed it. Some things take priority over insurrection.

The hot dog, as far as I know, is still in that gutter, or long since washed away, having accomplished nothing except giving us a story we'd tell for years, one that got progressively more elaborate with each telling—by the following weekend it was a foot-long, by the month after that there were two hot dogs, then a whole picnic's worth of ammunition hurled at us by an increasingly cartoonish set of assailants who, in our retelling, we always, always survived, unscathed and laughing, exactly as we had the first time.

# The Rusty Queer

Down at the end of Miller's Lane, past the collapsed fence and the tangle of blackberry brambles, there stood an old contraption that the neighborhood children had nicknamed "The Rusty Queer." No one quite remembered how it got there or what it was originally meant to do.

It looked like a cross between an old water pump and some kind of forgotten farm machine, its metal frame eaten through with decades of rust, painted in shades of orange and brown like autumn leaves that had turned to iron. Strange gears jutted out at odd angles, and a peculiar bell-shaped attachment hung from one side, though it hadn't rung in anyone's living memory.

Old Mr. Hendricks, who had lived on the lane longer than anyone, used to tell stories about it. He claimed his grandfather had said the thing once belonged to a traveling inventor who passed through town generations ago, leaving it behind when his cart broke down and he never returned to collect it. Whether the tale was true or just another piece of local folklore, no one could say for certain.

What made the machine truly queer wasn't just its strange design, but the way it seemed to attract odd little happenings. Children swore that on quiet evenings, if you pressed your ear against its rusted belly, you could hear a faint humming, almost like a tune trying to remember itself. Others claimed that fireflies gathered around it more thickly than anywhere else in the lane, blinking in patterns that seemed almost deliberate.

Eventually, the town considered hauling it away as scrap, but somehow it never happened. Perhaps it was sentiment, or perhaps it was simply that nobody wanted to be the one to disturb something so thoroughly, wonderfully strange. The Rusty Queer remained exactly where it was, a monument to mystery, quietly rusting into the landscape and into the stories that children would tell their own children one day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a queer couple getting harassed with a hot dog thrown from a truck in San Francisco, blending humor and vulnerability.
counterfactuals.output:
# Dolores Street, Late June

The hot dog arrives before the truck's rumble fades into traffic, a soft missile trailing mustard like a comet's tail, and for one absurd second we watch it arc—actually arc—through the fog-thin light, the whole city holding its breath around this ballistic frankfurter, this dollar-store javelin thrown by a boy who probably still sleeps with a nightlight.

It lands near my sneaker. Just sort of *plops*, apologetically, like even the hot dog knows this is embarrassing for everyone involved.

You laugh first. That's the thing about you—you always laugh first, like joy is a reflex you never unlearned, even now, even here, even with some kid leaning out a truck window to remind us that our hands finding each other on a sidewalk is apparently newsworthy, is apparently *worth the gas money* to drive by and hurl processed meat at.

We stand there. Two grown adults. A fallen soldier of a hot dog steaming faintly on the concrete like it, too, is embarrassed to be caught in this particular crossfire.

"Well," you say, "at least it wasn't a knish. That would've really hurt."

And I laugh, because you're right, because absurdity is the only language built for moments like this, because somewhere between the truck's taillights disappearing and the mustard congealing on the sidewalk, we have to decide: do we let this small violence sit in our chests like a stone, or do we let it become the story we tell at parties, the one where love survived a hot dog assault in the Mission, still holding hands, still walking toward wherever we were walking?

But underneath the laughter—you feel it too, I know you do—there's the old familiar flinch, the way our shoulders pull in half an inch, the way we both, without speaking, walk a little faster, a little closer, a little more like armor than skin.

This city that's supposed to be ours. This sidewalk we've walked a hundred times like it belonged to us because someone, once, bled and marched and died so it might.

Still: someone's kid, someone's nephew, someone's whole childhood of watching the wrong movies, leaning out a window with a hot dog like it's 1985 and we're still something to be afraid of, still something that warrants ammunition.

We keep walking. Your hand doesn't leave mine—not out of defiance, not exactly, though maybe a little defiance, mostly because leaving would mean the hot dog won, would mean some stranger's cruelty gets to write the ending of our Tuesday evening.

Instead we write it ourselves: two people, slightly shaken, still laughing, already turning this into myth, into dinner-party fodder, into *remember when*—

because that's what we do, we alchemists of small survivals, we transform the thrown thing into the story we choose to keep, the fear into the punchline, the flinch into just another kind of dance step, still moving forward, still tender, still—

impossibly, stubbornly—
in love
on a sidewalk
in a city
that sometimes forgets
whose ground this is.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a short piece of flash fiction narrated in first person about surviving a homophobic "gaybashing" incident that's absurd rather than violent, ending in a sex shop?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Great Silver Lake Ambush**

They came at me on a Tuesday, which already felt like poor planning on their part—Tuesdays are for laundry and existential dread, not hate crimes.

There were three of them, teenagers really, wearing matching windbreakers like they'd coordinated outfits for this but hadn't thought much beyond that. One held what I initially thought was a bat but turned out to be a rolled-up yoga mat someone's mother had probably asked him to bring in from the car.

"Hey f-faggot," the tallest one said, stumbling on the word like it was a vocabulary test he hadn't studied for.

"That's quite an opener," I said, still holding my iced oat milk latte, which I was not prepared to abandon under any circumstances.

The second kid pulled out his phone, presumably to film the incident, except his case was one of those glittery ones with a popsocket, and the whole phone slipped out of his hand and skittered across the pavement like a startled crab.

"Oh my god, Kevin," the third one hissed.

"Don't say my name!"

"I just said your name."

While Kevin scrambled after his phone, the yoga mat kid took a swing at me that was less "violent assault" and more "confused windmill," and the momentum sent him stumbling sideways into a fire hydrant. He yelped, grabbed his shin, and began hopping.

"This is going terribly," the third one said, to no one, to the universe.

I sipped my latte.

"Are you guys," I ventured, "doing okay?"

"We're bashing you!" Kevin said, phone finally reclaimed, though the screen was now spiderwebbed with cracks. "This is a bashing!"

"It's giving more like... interpretive dance."

The hydrant kid was still hopping. The third one had started nervously scrolling his own phone, possibly Googling "how long does a gaybashing take" or "am I allowed to leave."

Sensing the operation had lost all momentum, I did the only reasonable thing: I gestured for them to follow me, and—shockingly—they did, like ducklings who'd lost the will to be menacing. We walked half a block in silence until we arrived outside Rubber Rita's, the 24-hour pleasure emporium on the corner, its neon sign buzzing pink and blue against the dusk.

"Come on," I said, holding the door. "You clearly need better props."

Kevin looked at the yoga mat kid. The yoga mat kid looked at his shin. The third one just looked exhausted, like he'd signed up for a group project with people who hadn't read the material.

Inside, the fluorescent aisles hummed with the low murmur of vibrators charging on display, and Rita herself—six-foot-two in heels, reading glasses on a chain—glanced up from her crossword.

"Store's not really equipped for bashings, hon," she said. "Best I can do is a flogger. Educational, not offensive."

Kevin, to his credit, actually considered it.

I finished my latte. Somewhere outside, a car alarm went off, entirely unrelated, and none of us even flinched.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a literary, dreamlike vignette mixing mundane details like Woolite and insurance with a bizarre hate-crime attempt involving a hot dog, set in San Francisco's queer nightlife scene.
counterfactuals.output:
**Rinse Cycle**

The Woolite bottle sits on the windowsill like a small blue saint, watching me get ready. Cold water only, hand wash, lay flat to dry—I have followed none of these instructions in the four years I've owned this dress, and still it holds, still it shines under the bathroom light like something that trusts me more than I trust myself.

There is an insurance renewal notice folded into my clutch, because I am the kind of person who reads mail on the walk to the bus stop and then cannot bear to leave it at home, unopened, judging me. $340 a month for a body I mostly abuse with glitter and long nights. I fold it smaller. It becomes a kind of amulet.

The 14 Mission rattles past the Redwood Room, past the Café, past a man arguing with a parking meter about something that isn't the meter's fault. Dolores Street holds its jacarandas like a held breath. I get off two stops early because walking in these boots feels like a private ceremony, a way of arriving at myself before I arrive anywhere else.

Outside The Stud, the line curls around the block, all of us lit up like votive candles, waiting to be let into the dark. Someone's sequins are shedding a small gold weather onto the sidewalk. A drag king in a mustache made of actual eyebrow pencil is telling a story with her hands, and the hands are the story, really—the mouth is just where the sound comes out.

This is when the car slows.

It is a beige car. That's the detail I keep returning to, the dreamer's insistence on beige, on a Camry the color of dry oatmeal, windows down, bass thumping something with no real bassline, just percussion pretending to be conviction. A young man leans out. His face is doing the thing faces do when they've decided to become weapons—flattened, purposeful, already elsewhere.

He's holding a hot dog.

Not eating it. Holding it the way you'd hold a small torch, or a scepter improvised from a 7-Eleven counter, mustard-bright, bun soft as a threat that hasn't fully committed to being one. He says the word—the old word, the word that has followed people like me down more blocks than I can count, wearing different shoes each time—and he throws it.

It arcs. In the dream-logic of this street, in the particular slant of neon off the puddle by the curb, it arcs slow, almost apologetic, a comet made of ballpark condiments, and it lands three feet short of my patent leather boots, splitting open on the asphalt like a piñata that gave up early.

The car peels off. Somebody in line laughs—not at the violence, but at its failure, at the sheer physics of it, the way a threat can travel through the air and become, on impact, only lunch.

I look at the hot dog. It looks like it, too, cannot believe what it's been asked to be.

Inside, the bathroom mirror shows me nothing has changed. My mascara has not run. My dress, hand wash cold, lay flat to dry, is exactly as I left it this afternoon, drying over the shower rod while I stood in the kitchen reading about deductibles. I think about how insurance is a promise that says: something bad will happen, and here is the paperwork for after. There is no policy for this—for the mustard, for the word, for the particular tenderness of being hated so badly someone reaches for the nearest soft thing and hurls it, missing.

Someone hands me a wet napkin for my boots, though nothing touched them. It's the gesture that matters, the way care moves through a crowd like weather.

The DJ drops something with a bassline that actually commits. My friends pull me onto the floor, and the overhead lights turn everyone the color of forgiveness, or something close to it, and I dance like the Woolite bottle is still watching, like it might finally understand what it means to hold a thing gently, and still have it last.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a personal essay or prose poem where friends named Rusty, Josey, and Bob mock people who tried to gaybash the narrator, incorporating Astrud Gilberto's "Girl from Ipanema" playing in a sex shop.
counterfactuals.output:
# What They Didn't Know

The bell above the door of the shop on Fourth Street made its tinny sound, and inside, Astrud Gilberto was singing about the girl from Ipanema—that voice like something floating on water, tall and tan and young and lovely, going *ahh*—while Rusty leaned against the counter of dildos and leather and looked at my split lip like it was the funniest thing he'd seen all week.

"So let me get this straight," he said, and Josey groaned because Rusty always said that, every single time, *let me get this straight*, like it hadn't stopped being funny in 2003. "Three of them. Three grown men. Against you."

"I had a shoe," I said.

"You had a *shoe*," Bob repeated, delighted, like I'd said I had a battalion.

The record kept playing, all bossa nova cool, all Rio de Janeiro sun, completely unbothered by the fluorescent lights and the wall of butt plugs and the fact that I was standing there with an ice pack Josey had produced from somewhere, wrapped in a bandana that smelled like patchouli.

"And you *won*," Josey said. It wasn't a question. She said it the way you'd announce a war had ended.

"I wouldn't say *won*—"

"You're standing here. They're not." Bob crossed his arms. "That's winning. That's the whole ballgame."

Outside, the world continued to be the kind of place where men in a truck saw two people holding hands and decided that was an invitation, a provocation, an *opening*. They'd had numbers. They'd had the element of surprise. They had not accounted for the fact that I fight like someone who has spent a lifetime being underestimated, or that Josey, half a block back, screamed like a fire alarm going off in a library, or that the whole thing would end with me here, safe, ice on my face, listening to Astrud sing *ahh* like the world was gorgeous and gentle and full of nothing but longing.

"They're gonna go home," Rusty said, "and tell everyone how they got jumped by a fairy with a shoe."

"A *stiletto*," Josey corrected. "Have some respect for the weapon."

Bob was already laughing too hard to talk, doubled over near the rack of glitter-covered novelty items, and I realized I was laughing too, my split lip protesting, the ice slipping, the song moving into its outro, that soft impossible sway of it, and I thought: this is the part they never understand. That we would end up *here*. That there would be a *here* to end up in—a shop that smells like vanilla and vinyl, full of people who love me, put together like a search party, like a parade.

They wanted to make me small. Instead there was this: Rusty's ridiculous cackle, Josey re-icing my jaw with the tenderness of a nurse and the mouth of a sailor, Bob singing along badly with Astrud like he'd always known the words, and the four of us breaking into the kind of laughter that isn't about the joke at all, but about being alive to make it.

The girl from Ipanema kept walking. She never even looked. She didn't have to. That was always the secret—the walking away like nothing could touch you, like the whole world was just weather.

I finished my drink. My lip throbbed in time with the bassline.

I have never in my life felt so completely, ridiculously safe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
# What the Kimono Knew

The scarf came first—silk the color of a bruise healing, the kind of purple that means *almost better*. She'd found it in a thrift store on a Tuesday when nothing hurt yet, draped it over her shoulders like a promise she intended to keep. It smelled like someone else's grandmother. It felt like being held by a stranger who loved you anyway.

Thursday, the hot dog hit her collarbone. Someone's aim was bad or good, depending on how you counted victories. Relish sliding down like a small yellow insult. The boy who threw it was already running, already forgetting, already becoming the kind of man who tells this story at parties as if it were funny.

She stood in her doorway holding a paper towel to her shirt, and behind her, on the dresser, the rainbow arsenal caught the light—teal, magenta, one absurd glittering gold, arranged like a chorus line that had seen worse reviews. They didn't flinch. Objects don't know how to be afraid. This seemed, suddenly, like the only reasonable way to live.

*

Grief is surreal like that—it turns your bedroom into evidence, your body into a courtroom. The kimono scarf still hung on the doorknob, watching. Silk doesn't judge. Silk just is, the way tenderness just is, stubborn and available even when the world throws processed meat at your throat for the crime of walking home.

She thought: *they can hit me with a hot dog but they cannot touch the softness I have curated.* The dildos didn't care about optics. They existed in every color because someone, somewhere, decided joy should come in a spectrum, should refuse the binary of a single sad flesh-tone, should sit on a shelf gleaming like defiance you could hold in your hand.

*

By Friday she wore the scarf to the corner store, mustard stain be damned, tucked under her jacket like a secret organ. The clerk didn't notice. The world, mostly, doesn't notice—it's busy being cruel in small increments, is busy training boys to laugh at girls who love wrong, is busy pretending violence is just weather.

But here's what the hot dog didn't understand: it landed on skin that had been kissed by people who meant it. Skin that had draped itself in secondhand silk and new pleasure, unashamed. Skin that had already decided, long before Thursday, that softness was not surrender.

The scarf still smells like someone else's grandmother.
The dresser still glitters like a coronation.
She still walks home the long way, wearing color like armor,
because tenderness, it turns out,
is the strangest kind of revenge—

the kind that keeps choosing itself,
again,
gently,
gold.
